title: Groovy Exercises
description: Read each example in its lesson first. Predict the result, then check your answer. The notes explain the idea and one common mistake.

exercises.question: println prints a value with a newline. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: println writes the string and supplies a newline. Keep quotes around text.

exercises.question: def declares a variable without spelling its type. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: def declares the variable with value 3. Addition gives 5. Use numbers rather than quoted text for addition.

exercises.question: Double-quoted strings can place a variable in the text with a dollar sign. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The double-quoted string expands $name to Ravi. Single-quoted strings do not expand variables.

exercises.code:
def score = 8
if (score >= 5) { println "Pass" } else { println "Try again" }
exercises.question: if selects a block based on a rule. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The score test is true, so the first branch prints Pass. Use a clear comparison when testing a score.

exercises.question: A list stores ordered values. Its first position is zero. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The list puts dog at index 1 because indexing starts at zero. Position 1 is the second item.

exercises.code:
def book = [title: "Moon Trip", pages: 24]
println book.title
exercises.question: A map pairs keys with values. Dot syntax can read a simple text key. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: Dot syntax selects the title key from this map. A missing map value may be null; plan for that.

exercises.question: The range 1..3 includes both endpoints. each visits the values. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The inclusive range supplies 1, 2 and 3 to the closure. The ..< range leaves out its last endpoint.

exercises.code:
def twice = { n -> n * 2 }
println twice(4)
exercises.question: A closure is a block of reusable code. The arrow separates inputs from steps. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The closure input n receives 4. Its last expression returns 8. The last expression is the closure result.

exercises.question: collect builds a list from a closure result for each item. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: it is each current item. collect doubles both and stores the results. it names the input when you omit an explicit closure input.

exercises.question: findAll keeps items for which the closure result is true. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: findAll keeps the items whose rule result is true: 8 and 9. find reads one item, while findAll reads all matching items.

exercises.question: ?. skips a property read on null. The Elvis operator ?: supplies a fallback for a false-like value. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The safe call returns null instead of calling length. Elvis then supplies 0. Elvis uses Groovy truth, so it can replace empty strings and zero too.

exercises.question: A class groups data fields and actions. Groovy supports named property values during construction. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The named constructor inputs fill the title and pages properties. Spell property names exactly in the named arguments.
